course: AP Chemistry - Structure, Equilibrium and Energy
attribution: Original scope and sequence authored for the Luminfest Learning Harness, dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
scope: Structure only: concept titles, unit order and prerequisite intent. No third-party curriculum text is reproduced, and no restricted source is ingested.
description: A college-level chemistry course organised around the nine AP units: atomic structure and properties, compound structure, the properties of substances and mixtures, chemical reactions, kinetics, thermochemistry, equilibrium, acids and bases, and thermodynamics with electrochemistry. Each unit works from the particulate, symbolic and graphical representations an AP exam question moves between, and every quantitative claim is tied to the condition under which it holds.

concepts.title: The Mole and Molar Mass
concepts.summary: One mole contains 6.022 x 10^23 entities, and the molar mass in grams per mole is numerically equal to the average atomic or formula mass in u, so a measured mass becomes a particle count through one ratio.

concepts.title: Reading a Mass Spectrum
concepts.summary: Each peak of a mass spectrum sits at the mass of a single isotope and its relative height is that isotope fraction, so the peak pattern gives the element isotope composition without any chemical separation.

concepts.title: Average Atomic Mass from Isotope Abundances
concepts.summary: The average atomic mass is the sum of each isotope mass times its fractional abundance, so an element whose heaviest isotope dominates has a tabulated mass close to that isotope and never outside the isotope range.

concepts.title: Percent Composition from a Formula
concepts.summary: Percent composition is the total mass of one element in a mole of the compound divided by the molar mass, so for a pure compound it is fixed by the formula and independent of sample size.

concepts.title: Mass Percent of a Component in a Mixture
concepts.summary: A mixture mass percent is the mass of one component divided by the total mixture mass, and unlike percent composition it varies between samples because a mixture carries no fixed formula.

concepts.title: Coulomb's Law and Effective Nuclear Charge
concepts.summary: Coulomb's law makes the nucleus-electron attraction grow with the product of the charges and fall with the square of the separation, and because inner electrons shield incompletely the effective nuclear charge still rises left to right across a period.

concepts.title: Orbital Filling and Electron Configuration
concepts.summary: Electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbital available, filling 4s before 3d and leaving degenerate p orbitals singly occupied with parallel spins before any pairing, which is why a configuration predicts unpaired electrons and paramagnetism.
prerequisites: Coulomb's Law and Effective Nuclear Charge

concepts.title: Photoelectron Spectra and Subshell Energies
concepts.summary: Each photoelectron peak gives the binding energy of one subshell as the photon energy minus the ejected electron kinetic energy, and its area is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.

concepts.title: Radius and Ionization Energy Trends
concepts.summary: Atomic radius falls across a period as effective nuclear charge rises and grows down a group as shells are added, and first ionization energy follows the opposite pattern apart from two dips: group 13 loses a lone p electron from a higher sublevel and group 16 loses one electron of a paired set.

concepts.title: Valence Electrons and Main-Group Ion Charges
concepts.summary: Main-group atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration, so group 1 and 2 metals form 1+ and 2+ cations while group 16 and 17 nonmetals form 2- and 1- anions.

concepts.title: The Ionic-Covalent Continuum
concepts.summary: A bond is largely ionic once the electronegativity difference exceeds roughly 1.7 and largely covalent when the difference is small, so the two labels mark the ends of one continuum rather than two kinds of bond.

concepts.title: Bond Polarity and Molecular Dipole Moments
concepts.summary: A polar bond carries a dipole towards its more electronegative atom, but a molecule has a net dipole only when symmetry leaves the bond dipoles unable to cancel, which is why carbon dioxide is nonpolar.

concepts.title: Potential Energy Curves for Covalent Bonds
concepts.summary: A bond potential energy falls to a minimum at the equilibrium bond length and climbs steeply at shorter distances as the nuclei repel, so the depth of that well measures bond strength and, between the same two elements, a shorter equilibrium distance belongs to the deeper well.

concepts.title: Ionic Lattice Structure and Coordination
concepts.summary: An ionic solid is a three-dimensional lattice in which every ion is surrounded by counter-ions, and its lattice energy grows with the product of the ionic charges and shrinks as the ions become larger.

concepts.title: Metallic Bonding and Alloys
concepts.summary: Metal cations are held by a delocalised sea of valence electrons, which explains conductivity and malleability, and an alloy distorts that lattice by substituting or inserting atoms of a different size.

concepts.title: Drawing Lewis Diagrams
concepts.summary: A Lewis diagram is built by counting all valence electrons, bonding the skeleton with single bonds, completing outer octets, then placing any remainder on the central atom or forming multiple bonds until it reaches an octet.

concepts.title: Formal Charge and Resonance Hybrids
concepts.summary: Formal charge is the valence-electron count minus the electrons an atom owns in the diagram, and the preferred structure minimises it, while forms that differ only in electron placement are resonance contributors to one delocalised hybrid.

concepts.title: Electron-Domain Geometry and Molecular Shape
concepts.summary: Electron domains spread to the arrangement that maximises their separation, and a lone pair occupies more angular space than a bonding pair, so a tetrahedral domain set becomes trigonal pyramidal or bent when lone pairs are present.

concepts.title: Hybridization and Sigma versus Pi Bonds
concepts.summary: Mixing one s with one, two or three p orbitals gives sp, sp2 or sp3 hybrids whose directions match the observed linear, trigonal planar or tetrahedral angles, and the untouched p orbitals form the pi bond of a double or triple bond.

concepts.title: London Dispersion Forces and Polarizability
concepts.summary: Every pair of particles attracts through instantaneous dipoles, and the force strengthens with polarizability and contact area, which is why the halogens boil at higher temperatures down the group.

concepts.title: Hydrogen Bonding and Dipole-Dipole Forces
concepts.summary: A hydrogen bond is the attraction between hydrogen covalently bound to N, O or F and a lone pair on another such atom, strong enough to give water an unusually high boiling point and enthalpy of vaporisation.

concepts.title: Order in Crystalline and Amorphous Solids
concepts.summary: A crystalline solid has a repeating long-range lattice and melts at one temperature, while an amorphous solid lacks that order and softens over a range, so melting behaviour alone distinguishes the two.

concepts.title: Particulate Structure of the Three States
concepts.summary: Particles of a solid are fixed in place and only vibrate, particles of a liquid stay in contact but slide past one another, and particles of a gas are far apart and fill their container, so density and compressibility follow from the spacing.

concepts.title: Vapor Pressure and Boiling
concepts.summary: Vapor pressure rises with temperature as a larger fraction of molecules gains escape energy, and a liquid boils when that pressure equals the external pressure, which is why water boils below 100 degrees Celsius at altitude.
prerequisites: Particulate Structure of the Three States

concepts.title: The Ideal Gas Law
concepts.summary: The equation PV = nRT treats particles as point masses with no attractions, so it holds best at low pressure and high temperature and fails when particle volume and intermolecular attraction become significant.

concepts.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory and Molecular Speed
concepts.summary: Average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature, so at one temperature all gases share the same average kinetic energy while their root-mean-square speeds differ as the inverse square root of molar mass.

concepts.title: Real Gases Deviate in Both Directions
concepts.summary: For most gases at ordinary temperature, attractions pull the measured pressure below the ideal prediction while the particles own volume pushes it above, so the compressibility factor falls below one at moderate pressure and rises above one at high pressure.

concepts.title: Solutions Compared with Heterogeneous Mixtures
concepts.summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture whose components are dispersed at the particle level and cannot be separated by settling or filtering, while a heterogeneous mixture keeps visibly distinct regions that scatter light or settle on standing.

concepts.title: Molarity and Solution Representations
concepts.summary: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, so dissolving one mole of a strong electrolyte such as sodium chloride yields two moles of ions, and a particulate drawing must show that doubled count.

concepts.title: Separation by Distillation and Chromatography
concepts.summary: Distillation separates components by boiling point, while chromatography separates them by differing affinity for a mobile and a stationary phase, so each exploits a physical property rather than a reaction.

concepts.title: Solubility as a Saturation Equilibrium
concepts.summary: Solubility is the dissolved concentration in a saturated solution at a given temperature, and it is a property of the solute-solvent pair because the dissolution equilibrium shifts with temperature and with the solvent.

concepts.title: Spectra Record Absorbed and Emitted Photons
concepts.summary: A spectrum records the wavelengths a sample absorbs or emits, and because each transition needs a photon of matching energy, a line position identifies the species while a line intensity reports how much of it is present.

concepts.title: Photon Energy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
concepts.summary: A photon carries energy equal to h times its frequency, so ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to break some bonds, visible photons excite valence electrons and infrared photons only excite vibrations, which is why the spectral region fixes the kind of interaction.

concepts.title: The Beer-Lambert Law
concepts.summary: Absorbance equals molar absorptivity times path length times concentration, so a calibration curve at one wavelength converts an absorbance reading into an unknown concentration, provided the absorbing species and the instrument settings are unchanged.

concepts.title: What Counts as a Chemical Reaction
concepts.summary: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms so that existing bonds break and new ones form, which is why the same atoms appear on both sides of a balanced equation in different partnerships.

concepts.title: Writing Net Ionic Equations
concepts.summary: A net ionic equation keeps only the species that change, so ions appearing identically on both sides are cancelled as spectators and every strong electrolyte is written as its separated ions.

concepts.title: Representing a Reaction at the Particle Level
concepts.summary: The balanced equation, the particulate drawing and the net ionic equation describe one change at three levels, and any acceptable representation conserves both atoms and charge.

concepts.title: Distinguishing Physical from Chemical Change
concepts.summary: A physical change alters state or form without altering composition, while a chemical change produces new substances and is recognised by a colour change, gas evolution, precipitate or temperature change.

concepts.title: Mole Ratios and the Limiting Reactant
concepts.summary: Coefficients give the mole ratio linking any two species, and the limiting reactant is the one whose stoichiometric requirement runs out first, so it sets the maximum product while the excess reactant remains.

concepts.title: Percent Yield from the Limiting Reactant
concepts.summary: Percent yield is the actual product mass divided by the theoretical mass from the limiting reactant, so a result above 100 percent signals an impure or wet product rather than a better reaction.
prerequisites: Mole Ratios and the Limiting Reactant

concepts.title: Titration and the Equivalence Point
concepts.summary: A titration reaches equivalence when the added titrant moles match the stoichiometric requirement of the analyte, a point computed from the balanced equation that need not sit at neutral pH.

concepts.title: Precipitation, Acid-Base and Redox Classes
concepts.summary: A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble product from soluble ions, an acid-base reaction transfers a proton and a redox reaction changes oxidation numbers, so the class is identified by what is exchanged.

concepts.title: Proton Transfer in Acid-Base Reactions
concepts.summary: In an acid-base reaction a proton moves from the acid to the base, giving the conjugate base of the acid and the conjugate acid of the base, and the equilibrium favours the weaker acid and weaker base.

concepts.title: Assigning Oxidation Numbers and Balancing Redox
concepts.summary: Oxidation numbers follow fixed rules with oxygen at -2 and hydrogen at +1, and a redox equation balances once the electrons lost by oxidation equal the electrons gained by reduction.

concepts.title: Average and Instantaneous Rate
concepts.summary: Average rate is a concentration change over an interval while instantaneous rate is the tangent slope at one moment, so the two agree only when the rate is constant.

concepts.title: Rate Normalised by Stoichiometric Coefficients
concepts.summary: Dividing each species concentration change by its coefficient gives a single reaction rate, so a reactant consumed twice as fast as another still yields the same rate value.

concepts.title: Determining a Rate Law Experimentally
concepts.summary: A rate law is determined experimentally, not from the balanced equation, because the exponents reflect the mechanism slow step, so the orders come from varying one concentration at a time and comparing initial rates.

concepts.title: Reaction Orders and the Units of k
concepts.summary: The exponents sum to the overall order, and the units of the rate constant follow from that order, being per second for first order and per molar per second for second order.

concepts.title: Integrated Rate Laws and Half-Life
concepts.summary: An integrated rate law gives concentration as a function of time, and a first-order reaction has a half-life of 0.693 divided by the rate constant that does not depend on the starting concentration.

concepts.title: Molecularity of an Elementary Step
concepts.summary: An elementary step is classified by its molecularity as unimolecular, bimolecular or termolecular, and because the step happens as written its rate law follows from that molecularity rather than from experiment.

concepts.title: Collision Model and Activation Energy
concepts.summary: A collision reacts only if the molecules arrive with at least the activation energy and the right orientation, so heating raises the rate mainly by raising the fraction of collisions that clear the barrier rather than by raising the collision frequency.

concepts.title: Reaction Energy Profile and the Transition State
concepts.summary: A reaction energy profile plots potential energy along the reaction coordinate, its peak is the transition state, the reactant-to-peak gap is the activation energy and the reactant-to-product gap is the enthalpy change.

concepts.title: Mechanism Steps and the Slow Step
concepts.summary: A mechanism is a series of elementary steps that sum to the overall equation, and the slowest step controls the rate, so a rate law can be written from the reactants of that step alone.

concepts.title: Rate Law Derived from the Slow Step
concepts.summary: The rate law predicted by a mechanism uses the reactants of its slow step with that step's coefficients as exponents, so a predicted law that contradicts the measured one rules the mechanism out.

concepts.title: Pre-Equilibrium Approximation
concepts.summary: When a fast reversible step precedes the slow step, solving the fast step for the intermediate concentration and substituting it into the slow rate gives a rate law containing only species actually present.

concepts.title: Mechanisms on an Energy Diagram
concepts.summary: A multistep mechanism shows one peak per transition state on its energy profile, and the highest peak belongs to the slow step, so the diagram reveals which step gates the rate.

concepts.title: Catalysis and the Lower-Energy Pathway
concepts.summary: A catalyst supplies an alternative pathway of lower activation energy without being consumed, so it raises the rate in both directions and leaves the equilibrium constant and the enthalpy change unchanged.

concepts.title: Sign Conventions for Heat Flow
concepts.summary: An exothermic process releases heat and carries a negative enthalpy change because the system loses energy, while an endothermic process absorbs heat and carries a positive one, both at constant pressure.

concepts.title: Energy Diagrams and Enthalpy Change
concepts.summary: An energy diagram places the enthalpy of reactants and products on one vertical scale, so the difference is the enthalpy change and the barrier above the reactants is the activation energy.

concepts.title: Thermal Equilibrium and the Direction of Heat Flow
concepts.summary: Heat flows spontaneously from the hotter body to the colder one until both reach the same temperature, so at thermal equilibrium the net transfer is zero even though molecular collisions continue.

concepts.title: Specific Heat and Heat Capacity
concepts.summary: Specific heat is the energy needed to raise one gram of a substance by one kelvin, and the value 4.18 joules per gram kelvin for liquid water makes it a slow-warming reservoir that moderates climate and body temperature.

concepts.title: Coffee-Cup and Bomb Calorimetry
concepts.summary: Calorimetry finds the heat exchanged as mass times specific heat times the temperature change, with a coffee-cup calorimeter measuring at constant pressure so the heat equals the enthalpy change and a bomb calorimeter at constant volume so it equals the internal energy change.

concepts.title: Enthalpy of Phase Change and Heating Curves
concepts.summary: Melting and vaporisation absorb energy without raising the temperature, so a heating curve shows flat plateaus whose lengths are set by the enthalpy of fusion or vaporisation and by the sample mass.

concepts.title: Why Reaction Heats Are Tabulated as Enthalpies
concepts.summary: At constant pressure the heat exchanged by a reaction equals its enthalpy change, which is why reactions run in open vessels are tabulated as enthalpies rather than as internal energy changes.

concepts.title: Bond Enthalpies and Reaction Enthalpy
concepts.summary: A reaction enthalpy can be estimated as the bond enthalpies broken minus those formed, a route that works best for gas-phase reactions because bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds.

concepts.title: Formation Enthalpy and the Zero Convention
concepts.summary: The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states, so an element in its standard state has a formation enthalpy of exactly zero.

concepts.title: Hess's Law and Path Independence
concepts.summary: Because enthalpy is a state function, a reaction enthalpy is the same whatever sequence of steps connects reactants to products, so it can be assembled from reactions that are easier to measure.

concepts.title: Equal Forward and Reverse Rates
concepts.summary: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions run at equal rates, so concentrations stop changing although both reactions continue, and the state is reached from either direction.

concepts.title: Direction of Reversible Reactions
concepts.summary: A reversible reaction proceeds in the direction that lowers the system free energy until the reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant, after which no net change is observed.

concepts.title: Writing the Equilibrium Expression
concepts.summary: The equilibrium constant is the product of product concentrations raised to their coefficients divided by the same expression for reactants, with pure solids and liquids omitted because their concentrations are constant.

concepts.title: Comparing Q with K to Predict Direction
concepts.summary: The reaction quotient has the form of K but uses current concentrations, so Q below K drives the reaction forward, Q above K drives it in reverse and Q equal to K means the system is at equilibrium.

concepts.title: Calculating K from Equilibrium Data
concepts.summary: Substituting equilibrium concentrations into the expression gives K, whereas initial concentrations cannot be substituted unless the system has actually reached equilibrium.

concepts.title: Magnitude of K and the Extent of Reaction
concepts.summary: A K far above one means the reaction has run almost to completion, a K far below one means hardly any product forms, and a K near one leaves comparable amounts of both sides at equilibrium.

concepts.title: Rules for Combining Equilibrium Constants
concepts.summary: Reversing an equation inverts K, multiplying its coefficients raises K to that power and adding two equations multiplies their constants, so K is meaningful only for the equation as written at that temperature.

concepts.title: ICE Tables and the Small-x Approximation
concepts.summary: An ICE table derives each equilibrium concentration from the initial value and the stoichiometric change, and dropping x beside an initial concentration is valid only when x stays under about 5 percent of it.

concepts.title: Particulate and Graphical Views of Equilibrium
concepts.summary: At equilibrium a particulate drawing shows reactants and products present in unchanging numbers while collisions continue, and a concentration-time graph flattens at a nonzero value instead of reaching zero.

concepts.title: Le Chatelier's Response to a Disturbance
concepts.summary: A system at equilibrium shifts to partly offset a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, but only a temperature change alters the value of K itself.

topics.topic: Reaction Quotient and Le Châtelier's Principle

concepts.title: Explaining a Shift with the Reaction Quotient
concepts.summary: Adding a reactant or removing a product makes Q smaller than K so the forward reaction dominates, and compressing a gas mixture shifts it towards the side with fewer gas moles because that direction drives Q below K.

concepts.title: Ksp and Molar Solubility
concepts.summary: The solubility product is the product of the ion concentrations in a saturated solution each raised to its coefficient, so molar solubility follows from Ksp through the salt stoichiometry.

concepts.title: The Common-Ion Effect
concepts.summary: Adding an ion the dissolving salt already produces pushes Q above Ksp, so solid precipitates until Q returns to Ksp and the salt solubility is lower than in pure water.

concepts.title: Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis Definitions
concepts.summary: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and a base accepts one, while the Lewis definition widens acids to electron-pair acceptors so that a species without hydrogen, such as boron trifluoride, still counts as an acid.

concepts.title: Conjugate Pairs and Amphiprotic Species
concepts.summary: Every Bronsted-Lowry acid has a conjugate base differing by one proton, and a species such as water or the hydrogen carbonate ion can donate or accept a proton depending on its partner.

topics.topic: pH and pOH of Strong Acids and Bases

concepts.title: pH, pOH and the Water Ion Product
concepts.summary: pH is the negative base-ten logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, and at 25 degrees Celsius pH plus pOH equals 14 because the ion product of water is 1.0 x 10^-14.

concepts.title: Ka, Kb and the Conjugate Relationship
concepts.summary: Ka measures the extent of weak-acid ionisation and Kb the extent for its conjugate base, and their product equals the water ion product, so a stronger acid always has a weaker conjugate base.

concepts.title: Solving Weak-Acid Equilibrium Problems
concepts.summary: Combining Ka with an initial concentration and an unknown x gives the hydrogen ion concentration, and the shortcut that neglects x fails once x exceeds about 5 percent of the initial concentration, which happens for a relatively strong weak acid or a very dilute solution.
prerequisites: Ka, Kb and the Conjugate Relationship

concepts.title: Neutralization and Buffer Formation
concepts.summary: Adding a limited amount of strong base to a weak acid converts part of it into its conjugate base, so the mixture left behind holds the acid and conjugate base pair a buffer requires.

concepts.title: Titration Curves and the Half-Equivalence Point
concepts.summary: On a weak-acid titration curve the pH at half-equivalence equals the acid pKa because acid and conjugate base are then equimolar, and the steepest segment of the curve brackets the equivalence point.

topics.topic: Molecular Structure of Acids and Bases

concepts.title: Inductive and Resonance Effects on pKa
concepts.summary: Electron-withdrawing atoms or groups stabilise the conjugate base and lower pKa, which is why trichloroacetic acid is far stronger than acetic acid and why an oxyacid strengthens as its central atom becomes more electronegative.

concepts.title: Comparing pH with pKa
concepts.summary: When the pH is below an acid pKa the protonated form dominates and when it is above the pKa the deprotonated form dominates, so comparing the two numbers predicts the charge of the species in solution.

concepts.title: How a Buffer Responds to Added Acid or Base
concepts.summary: A buffer neutralises added strong acid with its basic component and added strong base with its acidic component, so the pH moves only slightly until one member of the pair is used up.

concepts.title: Buffers and the Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
concepts.summary: A buffer holds a weak acid and its conjugate base in comparable amounts, and its pH equals the acid pKa plus the logarithm of the base-to-acid ratio, so the ratio rather than the absolute amounts sets the pH.

concepts.title: Buffer Capacity and Effective Range
concepts.summary: A buffer works within roughly one pH unit of its acid pKa, and its capacity grows with the absolute concentrations of the pair, so a buffer of correct ratio but low concentration fails on adding strong acid.

concepts.title: pH-Dependent Solubility of Salts
concepts.summary: The solubility of a salt whose anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid rises in acidic solution, because protonating the anion removes it and pulls the dissolution equilibrium towards dissolving.

concepts.title: Entropy and Microstates
concepts.summary: Entropy measures the number of microstates available to a system, so a process that spreads matter or energy over more arrangements has a positive entropy change, as when a solid melts or a gas expands into a vacuum.

concepts.title: Absolute Entropy and the Third Law
concepts.summary: The third law sets the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero to zero, so tabulated absolute entropies let a reaction entropy change be taken as products minus reactants without any arbitrary reference point.

topics.topic: Gibbs Free Energy and Thermodynamic Favorability

concepts.title: Gibbs Free Energy as the Favorability Criterion
concepts.summary: The free energy change equals the enthalpy change minus temperature times the entropy change, and at constant temperature and pressure a negative value means the forward process is thermodynamically favoured while zero means equilibrium.

concepts.title: Temperature Dependence of Favorability
concepts.summary: An endothermic reaction with a positive entropy change becomes favourable only above the temperature at which T times the entropy change exceeds the enthalpy change, so the sign pair decides whether a reaction is always, never or sometimes favourable.
prerequisites: Gibbs Free Energy as the Favorability Criterion

concepts.title: Thermodynamic versus Kinetic Control
concepts.summary: A reaction under thermodynamic control yields the more stable product, while under kinetic control the faster-forming product dominates, so the product distribution depends on temperature and on how long the reaction is allowed to run.

concepts.title: Free Energy and the Equilibrium Constant
concepts.summary: The standard free energy change equals minus RT times the natural logarithm of K, so a large negative value corresponds to a large equilibrium constant and a reaction that runs nearly to completion.

concepts.title: Free Energy of Dissolution
concepts.summary: Dissolution must supply the lattice enthalpy and is repaid by the hydration enthalpy, and the sum corrected by the entropy gain of dispersing the ions decides whether the salt dissolves at all.

concepts.title: Coupled Reactions
concepts.summary: A thermodynamically unfavourable reaction can be driven by coupling it to a favourable one whose free energy release exceeds the cost, as ATP hydrolysis does for the reactions of a cell.

concepts.title: Anode, Cathode and Electron Flow
concepts.summary: In any electrochemical cell oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, electrons travel through the external circuit from anode to cathode, and ions carry the current through the salt bridge or electrolyte.

concepts.title: Cell Potential and the Sign of Free Energy
concepts.summary: The standard cell potential is the cathode reduction potential minus the anode reduction potential, and a positive potential corresponds to a negative free energy change because that change equals minus nFE.

concepts.title: Nernst Equation and Nonstandard Potential
concepts.summary: Cell potential falls as the reaction quotient rises, following a potential equal to the standard potential minus RT over nF times the natural logarithm of Q, which at 25 degrees Celsius becomes the standard potential minus 0.0592 over n times log Q.

concepts.title: Electrolysis and Faraday's Law
concepts.summary: An electrolytic cell uses an external voltage to drive a nonspontaneous reaction, and the moles of substance deposited equal the charge passed divided by nF, so the charge alone fixes the mass produced.
